The Crowned rockcod Trematomus scotti is a benthic nototheniid that inhabits the continental shelf waters of Antarctica, where it occupies a relatively high trophic position within the cryopelagic food web. Field surveys conducted during the austral summer indicate that sexually mature adults attain a maximum total length of 24.7 centimeters [Li = 24.7 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the medium-bodied nototheniids of the Southern Ocean. This ultimate length is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory characteristic of high-latitude fishes. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual reaching this size is 132.8 grams [Wwi = 132.8 grams], a body mass that reflects the considerable energy reserves necessary for overwintering survival and reproductive investment under the extreme seasonal constraints of polar environments. Juvenile specimens collected from sub-ice platelet layers demonstrated a length-weight relationship consistent with that of congeners, suggesting a common allometric pattern within the genus. The relatively modest maximum body size compared to other nototheniids is likely an adaptation to the limited and pulsed food availability that typifies the Antarctic continental shelf ecosystem.

Puberty in Trematomus scotti is attained upon reaching a total length of 13.5 centimeters [Lp = 13.5 centimeters], a morphological milestone that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 19.3 grams [Wwp = 19.3 grams]. These values were derived from gonadal histology of field-caught specimens during a multi-year monitoring program at McMurdo Sound. The length at first maturity represents approximately 55 percent of the ultimate total length, a ratio consistent with the life-history strategy of many iteroparous nototheniids that allocate substantial somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive effort. At this developmental stage, the fish undergo a suite of physiological changes including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Males exhibit testicular maturation characterized by the proliferation of spermatogonia and subsequent spermiation. The energetic investment required to reach this reproductive threshold is considerable, particularly given the constraints of a cold, nutrient-poor environment where metabolic rates are low but digestive efficiency is limited.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by the thermal conditions of the Southern Ocean. At a water temperature of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C], females release approximately 14 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 14 eggs per spawning event] and produce roughly 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per year], values inferred from observed ovarian follicle dynamics and batch fecundity counts in gravid individuals. This modest reproductive output reflects the slow metabolic pace imposed by life at subzero temperatures. The spawning period is protracted, with vitellogenic oocytes developing over many months before final maturation is triggered by seasonal photoperiod cues. Batch spawning is likely the predominant reproductive mode, with individual females releasing multiple clutches over the course of the austral summer. The low environmental temperature profoundly affects all aspects of gametogenesis, including the rate of yolk deposition and the timing of oocyte final maturation. Comparisons with the congener Trematomus bernacchii suggest that thermal regime is a primary determinant of ovarian recrudescence rates in both species.

The early life history of Trematomus scotti is closely tied to the seasonal availability of sea ice and the associated microbial and zooplankton communities. Yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs following an incubation period of 95 days [ab = 95 days] at a stable temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C], a duration that permits slow, thorough development of organ systems prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth is 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a mass consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters that characterizes this species. Following the absorption of the yolk sac, the free-swimming larva must encounter suitable planktonic prey within a narrow temporal window to avoid reaching the point of no return. At the subzero ambient temperatures that dominate the pelagic larval phase, metabolic demands are minimized, but the low prey densities typical of the early spring plankton bloom pose a significant challenge to first-feeding success.

Longevity data for Trematomus scotti are derived from otolith annulus counts and mark-recapture studies conducted over multiple decades at nearshore Antarctic monitoring stations. Under the ambient thermal conditions of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C], the lifespan reaches approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years], placing this species among the longer-lived nototheniids of the continental shelf. This extended longevity is a common life-history feature of polar fishes and is underpinned by extremely slow senescence rates that are thought to be physiologically linked to low metabolic activity and reduced oxidative damage at subzero tissue temperatures. Mortality in older individuals is primarily attributed to predation by seals and large nototheniids, as well as the energetic costs associated with successive spawning seasons. The species exhibits a gradual, age-related decline in reproductive performance rather than a rapid, semelparous death following a single spawning event.
